nytimes.com.title: People of All Ages Join French Student Protests as Movement Broadens
nytimes.com.text:
Labor activists, teachers, parents and university students turned out by the thousands on Tuesday to join high school students in demonstrations that swept across France, adding an intergenerational range of voices to demands that government fix ailing schools.
The largest crowds massed in Paris, where thousands of students and their supporters marched about two miles from République to Nation, two of the city’s main squares, protesting school understaffing, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings, among other complaints.
“Hitting the young amounts to insulting the future,” one sign read, while another said, “I don’t want to be another brick in the wall.”
In spite of a heavy police presence, the mood at the Paris protest was cheerful. The government estimated that 56,000 people took part, among 256,000 demonstrating nationwide; a major labor union cited a national figure more than twice as large.
Catherine Jegou, 61, a middle schoolteacher and member of a union of school workers, said she had come to support the high school students, whose demands echoed those of teachers. “For years we have demanded that the public school system have more means,” she said.

nytimes.com.title: The Fight for Britain’s Right: Can Kemi Badenoch Reboot the Conservatives?
nytimes.com.text:
Plain-speaking, confident and buoyed by rising personal ratings, Kemi Badenoch has gained a tight grip on Britain’s main opposition Conservative Party since she became its leader in 2024, following its disastrous general election defeat.
But as she prepared for a keynote speech on Wednesday at her party’s annual conference in Birmingham, England, Ms. Badenoch, who is the first Black leader of a major British political party, faces battles on two fronts.
Despite her own improved ratings, the Conservatives are less popular with voters, surveys suggest, than when they suffered their catastrophic election loss in 2024. According to opinion polls they trail not just the governing Labour Party — rejuvenated under its recently-installed leader, Prime Minister Andy Burnham — but also the right-wing populist Reform U.K. party, led by Nigel Farage.
Mr. Farage has had a rocky few months, with questions swirling about his finances and those of his party, but Reform’s support in the polls still hovers at around 22 percent, about five percentage points above the Tories.
The fractures on Britain’s political right could help the Labour Party in the next general election, analysts say, which must be called by 2029 but could come sooner.
“Farage has not yet conceded that he can’t kill the Conservatives and perhaps still hopes that he can,” said Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London. “And Badenoch shows no signs of wanting to do a deal with Reform, at least before the election."

nytimes.com.title: F.B.I. Charges American in Plot Behind Canada’s Tumbler Ridge School Shooting
nytimes.com.text:
The U.S. authorities arrested a 30-year-old Washington State resident on Tuesday on charges of conspiring to commit a school shooting in rural British Columbia, eight months after a Canadian teenager killed eight people.
On Feb. 10, Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, shot and killed her mother and 11-year-old stepbrother in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, a tranquil mountain town. She then went to the local school and shot and killed five students and one educational instructor. She died in the school of a self-inflicted gunshot wound, and her death prompted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to announce they were not searching for any other suspects.
But on Tuesday afternoon, officials from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the U.S. Department of Justice announced that another person had, for months, been in contact with Ms. Van Rootselaar to plot the shooting. That included sending cash — about $100 for a pair of loafers and $15 for a lighter — to Ms. Van Rootselaar, as well as dispensing technical advice on how to carry out the attacks.
The suspect, identified by the police as James Cody Bryant, of Bellingham, Wash., was arrested on Tuesday morning, the authorities said at a Seattle news conference. Officials said that the suspect, who was born male and was referred to by authorities with male pronouns, identifies as female, similar to the shooter, Ms. Van Rootselaar.
Ms. Van Rootselaar and the suspect met about three years ago on Omegle, a chat website that connects strangers. After the website shut down in 2023 amid criticism that it was a haven for sexual abuse, the pair kept in touch, said Mike Harrington, a special agent in charge of the F.B.I. Seattle field office.
Their friendship developed over conversations about planning the shooting that began at least six months before the attacks, including communication on Discord, a social media platform. Ms. Van Rootselaar was also active on various other social media accounts, where she documented her fascination with firearms and her mental health issues, for which she took prescribed medications and experimented with psychedelic drugs and other illegal substances.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s ‘for you’ presidency became all about himself. It’s hurting the GOP
cnn.com.text: The ad that defined the 2024 election said “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” Two years on, it’s mostly about him. The scathing jab at the Democratic nominee did not just attack her positions on transgender issues. It positioned her opponent as the only one listening to Americans’ pleas for help with high food and housing prices. But a return to the gold-draped Oval Office and a personal construction spree immortalizing his legacy seem to have distracted President Donald Trump from such concerns — which in some ways have gotten worse as a result of his policies. And Trump’s accelerated campaign swing, so far stopping in Texas, Ohio, Alabama and Nebraska — ostensibly meant to help GOP midterm election candidates — is featuring undisciplined and self-referential appearances that trigger political firestorms but produce few answers to the critical question of the election. In recent days, Trump trampled his party’s campaign message by igniting a furor over whether he’d suggested Iran could “take out” San Diego or Los Angeles. Democrats’ responses did not accurately reflect the context. But his intemperance gave them a chance to dominate the narrative on one of the declining days before the election. Trump is also bitterly complaining that Fox News isn’t being fair. He launched another controversy by using taxpayer cash for campaign-style ads; used an anti-transgender slur against a Democratic candidate in South Carolina; and told a weekend crowd in Ohio the GOP would shove an election win up the rival party’s “ass.” Touting a shipbuilding project Tuesday in Maryland, he bafflingly extemporized about rechristening the “fake media” the “artificial” media after freeing up the word by dubbing artificial intelligence “super intelligence.” Letting Democrats off the hook Trump has never stuck to the script. In fact, his verbal improvisations have often been a political strength. Yet the off-the-cuff riffs and taunts that once marked him as the ultimate outsider eviscerating the political system now risk becoming a liability as voters blame him for high prices, a Middle East quagmire and their thwarted hopes. And in a midterm election turning on the unpopularity of his presidency and apparent denial over the haves-and-have-nots economy, his intensifying campaign blitz — mostly so far in red states — seems to lack a strategy. There’s also no evidence it’s having the intended impact, though he claimed on Truth Social on Tuesday that he was “flipping races all over the place.” Four weeks from an election in which Democrats only need a handful of seats to win back the House, and as a close battle for the Senate goes down to the wire, Trump is being as good as his word to make the campaign about him. And he may be letting Democrats — who still lack voters’ trust, polls show — off the hook. He’s siding with tech billionaires in telling Americans they must embrace AI data centers, which many voters loathe for their vast footprint on the landscape and for guzzling electricity and water. During a trip to boost Republicans in Nebraska on Monday, he seemed unsympathetic to ranchers angry at his move to pause tariffs on tens of thousands of tons of foreign beef to bring national prices down, saying they’d be in “big trouble if Democrats win.” In Baltimore on Tuesday, he boasted about stocks that keep hitting record highs — benefiting the richest Americans most. And he told families who dread every visit to a gas station that it’s a “small price to pay” to keep Iran from gaining a nuclear weapon — though he’d claimed to have obliterated Tehran’s nuclear capacity before launching the war. When the president does have good news to tout, such as the $5 billion infrastructure investment by South Korea’s Hanwha Group in Philadelphia, he styles it as a personal triumph rather than embroidering a narrative about how such successes can create an economy that helps working Americans. His scattershot method rarely shows off achievements like higher-than-expected tax refunds and initiatives to cut the cost of medicine and housing in their best light. ‘Living in a bubble’ Incumbent presidents always face a balancing act in midterms, especially when voters blame them for economic conditions. But rather than explaining the reality and offering ways to improve it, the president often conjures a fresh one. “This is the golden age of America,” he said Tuesday. “We’re doing numbers that nobody ever thought were possible.” This doesn’t only ignore polls like one released Sunday by CBS/YouGov that found 70% of voters think his policies are hiking grocery prices. It’s a gift for Democrats when gasoline averages $4.36 a gallon, diesel is around $6.30 a gallon and mortgage rates just topped 7%. “The president is showing, which is not unusual, that he is living in a bubble,” Michigan Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell told CNN’s Audie Cornish on Monday, specifically referring to AI data centers but exemplifying Trump’s wider issues. Whether he’s foisting weak candidates on Republicans in states such as Texas and Georgia or insisting that his party elevate a president with an approval rating in the 30s, Trump’s entire approach to the midterms seems unwise. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” the president pleaded with voters at his rally in Alabama last week, delighting Democratic strategists. But could there be some method in his maelstrom? Time catches up with every political leader Trump would probably be wasting his time by wooing moderate and independent voters as polls show them drifting away. In swing Senate races in places like Maine, Michigan and Georgia, he might do the GOP more harm than good. If polls can be believed that there are tight contests in states — such as Ohio and Iowa — that Trump won by double digits two years ago, reviving that almost mystical connection with the base might offer his party the only viable form of triage. “Democrats have placed President Trump on the ballot,” Pennsylvania Rep. Ryan Mackenzie told CNN’s Manu Raju on Tuesday. “What we need, and what I think the president is saying … is that we need Republicans to see that he is going to be on the ballot in the sense that his policies and his agenda are going to be on the ballot.” During the 2016 campaign, the chaos was not a turnoff but an asset. Trump’s untamed nature, insults and absurd digressions eviscerated mores his supporters hated. Everyone in politics thought he’d destroyed his own campaign by denigrating the Vietnam War heroism of Sen. John McCain. But the episode showed instead that Trump was ahead of the curve, and political and media elites hadn’t realized he’d changed the game. Back then, Trump would scour his crowds to test reactions to his most outrageous lines. The rallies often felt like a night at a party when someone was saying stuff many people agreed with but wouldn’t dare blurt out. When Trump goes off on a rant now, he may be trying to recapture that magic. But circumstances have changed a decade later. Trump isn’t the outsider now; he is the establishment figure waging a poorly explained war and driving up prices, despite his attempts to show he’s not relinquished his rebel spirit. His political longevity is extraordinary. But the gap between Trump’s “golden age” and the lived reality of many of his supporters is described by high housing and grocery prices. His base also appears to be narrowing, as CNN’s Aaron Blake noted Tuesday, citing New York Times/Siena College polls showing between 9% and 16% of Republican voters saying they favored the Democratic nominee in key states Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. Polls can change in the final days, and on November 3, they won’t matter. That’s when voters will answer the question defining Trump’s 2026 campaign. Was it all about them? Or him?

cnn.com.title: France’s student protests highlight a debt crisis that could spill over to the rest of Europe
cnn.com.text: France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit. The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency. The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike. At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense. High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure. Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023. Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics. The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said. “Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.” Bond yield blowout Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields. The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative. The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s. Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN. These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level. Beyond France, risks loom large The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany. Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month. “(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note. High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however. If governments don’t cut spending, “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN. Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further. Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads. Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

cnn.com.title: Israel marks three years since October 7 attack with memorials and protests
cnn.com.text: Three years to the minute after the start of the deadliest single day in Israel’s history, the country marked the somber occasion with a series of ceremonies, memorials and protests at more than 400 locations. At 6:29 in the morning on October 7, 2023, Hamas-led gunmen stormed Israeli communities along the border with the Gaza Strip, killing more than 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages to the enclave. Those slain included children, women, elderly people and complete families. The commemoration began with a national moment of silence at the time the attack started. At noon, bereaved families and civil grassroot protest groups will hold a national minute of reflection, joined by various public hospitals, local municipalities, universities and private businesses. Memorial events will also take place at the Nova festival site in the Re’im Forest, where over 370 people were murdered and 44 were abducted. Additional protest convoys and displays are expected throughout the country all day. Shir Mathias, whose parents Shachar and Shlomi Mathias were killed during the attack on Kibbutz Holit on the Gaza border, called Tuesday for a change in the country’s leadership. “Just before we enter October 7, I have one message,” she wrote on X. “Everyone who had their hand on the wheel, those in uniforms and suits alike — must go home. I call on all citizens of Israel, change your profile picture to the most self-evident message: ‘Everyone must go home.’” On Wednesday evening, a national memorial ceremony will be held in Tel Aviv, and tens of thousands are expected to attend. The event is organized by the “Kumu” movement (“Rise Up” in Hebrew), which represents October 7 survivors and victims’ families, and will be hosted by former hostage Eli Sharabi and actress Shani Cohen. Israel held its official state memorials on Monday. “Even three years after the outbreak of the war — when the State of Israel is stronger than ever — the terrible hours of the Simchat Torah attack remain seared within us,” said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, referencing the Jewish holiday on which the attack happened. At a cabinet meeting one day later, Netanyahu foreshadowed more war ahead, despite a stalled US-brokered ceasefire agreement one year ago. He said Israel has killed “4,000 out of 6,000” militants who infiltrated Israel on October 7, 2023. “We will reach all of them,” he said, amid near daily Israeli strikes in Gaza. Since the start of the war, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in the strip. In contrast to the official ceremonies, most of Wednesday’s commemoration events are grassroots efforts, organized by survivors and victims of the October 7 attack, including the October Council and the Kumu movement. A recurring demand by both groups is to establish a state commission of inquiry, the most powerful investigative mechanism in Israeli law empowered to examine national-level disasters and decisions. Netanyahu has consistently resisted such calls for three years and has not appointed any other special inquiry to investigate the failures that day. Einav Zangauker, mother of freed hostage Matan Zangauker and one of the most vocal critics of the government, wrote Tuesday on X: “Three years since the day that changed my life and our lives as a people. Three years of loss and pain. Three years of a basic demand for accountability. For those we lost, for those who returned and whose lives were changed forever, and for a country that deserves hope and repair.” The anniversary falls less than three weeks from the October 27 election in which accountability has become a central campaign issue. Netanyahu’s rivals have stepped up their criticism and have turned the anniversary into to a focal point of their campaign, especially after a string of media reports alleging that Israel received preliminary warnings from the United Arab Emirates and Egypt ahead of the attack. “This is a very deep failure,” said Gadi Eisenkot, currently polling as Netanyahu’s main challenger in the elections. He accused the prime minister of dodging a state commission of inquiry. “Netanyahu knows better than anyone why he is running from the truth, why he wants to bury the truth,” he said at a recent conference. Eisenkot, whose son was killed in Gaza during the war, will spend the day visiting Israeli communities along the Gaza border, as will former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, another Netanyahu rival.

cnn.com.title: Takeaways: Trump and abortion rights take center stage in first Maine Senate debate
cnn.com.text: GOP Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, sparred over President Donald Trump and abortion rights in their first debate Tuesday night in Maine’s all-important Senate race with control of the chamber at stake. Appearing in Portland, the state’s largest city, the two had a spirited — but civil — debate that displayed two very different strategies. Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, touted her “effective leadership” securing federal funds for Maine, while Jackson sought to nationalize the race with persistent criticism of her relationship with Trump and 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who later voted to overturn the federal right to an abortion. “Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?” Jackson asked, days after Justice Samuel Alito told CBS News he’s “thought about” retiring. Collins repeatedly pitched herself as unusually independent among lawmakers and cast doubt on the notion that Trump would want to visit Maine to stump for her. “I’m not exactly his favorite senator,” she said. It was the first of four debates the two candidates are scheduled to do over 10 days. Collins is a top Democratic target in the midterms, seeking reelection in a state that Trump lost three times. Democrats picked Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, to replace Graham Platner as their nominee in July after Platner dropped out over a rape allegation, which he denies. The race took another turn in recent days after the publication of a ProPublica story alleging a pay-to-play scheme involving Collins’ office. She said at the debate that the allegations were “completely false” and “very offensive.” Jackson said it showed how “politicians are bought and paid for.” Jackson blames Trump, Collins blames state Dems Jackson repeatedly sought to make Trump a liability for Collins, while Collins worked to tie him to the Democratic-led legislature in Augusta. He served in the Maine House – and then Senate – from 2002-2024, and Collins took several opportunities to remind viewers of his long tenure. Jackson accused Collins multiple times of voting “96% of the time” with Trump and of not doing enough to push back against his tariffs, immigration policies and the war in Iran. Collins detailed how she split with Trump on those issues, like getting tariff exemptions for certain products important to Maine, but Jackson scoffed at her answers. “Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” Jackson said. At one point, Collins took issue with the methodology of the study that she said Jackson had been citing for the 96% figure. He brushed it off, saying, “Whatever, it’s far too often.” Collins was far more interested in talking about Augusta than Trump. She argued, for example, that Democratic state lawmakers were responsible for Maine having the “fourth highest electricity rates in the country.” “If you look at the policies that have driven up the cost of living in Maine, you have to look at Augusta,” Collins said. “Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson.” Focus on abortion rights Jackson and his allies made little secret of his strategy going into the debate: Ramp up pressure on Collins, who has long billed herself as supportive of abortion rights, to answer for her Kavanaugh vote. This week is the eight-year anniversary of the vote. Jackson brought it up within seconds of his opening statement and later seized on the topic when given the chance to pose a question to Collins. “What will it take for you to admit that you were wrong [on Kavanaugh]?” Jackson asked. Collins gave a defense of her vote that has become well-rehearsed throughout the race. She said she “clearly” disagreed with his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade but said it would have been “inappropriate” to ask him during the confirmation process how he would vote on a particular issue. She did concede, however, that she did not like that he called Roe v. Wade settled law – because, she said, “to me, that meant that it would not be overturned.” Notably, Collins sought to flip the issue on Jackson, bringing up a series of anti-abortion positions he took early in his political career that he has since disavowed. “There’s only one of us on this stage who has aways been pro-choice, and that’s me,” Collins said. Jackson did not take the bait. “She doesn’t regret the vote” for Kavanaugh, he said, calling it “incredible that she will not admit to being wrong.” Getting to know Jackson While Susan Collins has been in the Senate since 1997, Jackson is newer to the national scene, and some Democrats are still getting to know him. Even his supporters acknowledge he is not as strong of a speaker – or personality – as Platner, though they share similar working-class progressive politics. The often casually clad Jackson wore a suit to the debate, and while he appeared to go after Collins more than she targeted him, he kept his attacks tightly focused on issues around Trump and abortion and did not come across as overzealous. The debate ended on a lighthearted note as the two joked about their favorite football teams. Jackson is one of the most progressive Democratic nominees in a battleground Senate race this cycle, and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont is set to visit Maine this weekend to hold three rallies for him. Like Sanders, Jackson is a proponent of the universal health care program Medicare for All. Asked about his support for Medicare for All and his thoughts on democratic socialists – the label that Sanders uses — Jackson chose to respond to the former part of the question and not the latter. “I support Medicare for All so that people I know across the state have health care,” Jackson said, adding that “Republicans, Democrats, independents all across the state” are backing his campaign. Collins criticized Medicare for All, saying Jackson wants “Big Government to take over the entire health care service.” They also split sharply during a lightning round of questions where they were asked if voters should show identification to cast a ballot. “No,” Jackson said. “As a working logger, many times I went to the polls without my ID.” Collins was just as explicit in the other direction. “Yes,” she said, “Only Americans should vote in American elections.”

cnn.com.title: Scientists name ancient crocodile species found in rock that built the Great Sphinx
cnn.com.text: The croc family tree may be getting a new branch. Analyzing fossilized remains discovered in the same bedrock that built the Great Sphinx, paleontologists newly identified a crocodilian species that once roamed a shallow sea in what’s now Egypt about 45 million years ago. The Mokattam Formation in northern Egypt is a thick layer of limestone that has preserved prehistoric marine fossils, including fish, sharks and early whales. That same limestone outcrop also provided much of the raw material ancient Egyptians used to build some of their most famous monuments, including the Great Sphinx and the pyramids at Giza. Now, scientists have identified the extinct crocodile species that lived millions of years before the Egyptians built the structures. Not only do the crocodile specimens share the same geologic foundation as the iconic landmarks, but one of the key fossils, a nearly complete skull, bears a striking resemblance to the Sphinx: The skull, first unearthed in the 1920s, is missing the tip of its snout similar to the Sphinx statue, which famously lost its nose. This coincidental trait inspired researchers to name the new genus Herugavialis after Heru, or Horus, the Egyptian god associated with the construction of the mythical creature. The species discovery adds to scientists’ understanding of the diversity and history of gharials, a group of crocodilians with a complicated evolutionary history, according to the authors of a study published Tuesday in the journal Royal Society Open Science. “Herugavialis cairensis is one of the six species of gharials that we see in the Mediterranean across a 43 million year period, from 66-23 million years ago. Of course, there could be even more species that we just don’t know about yet,” said co-lead study author Paul Burke, a vertebrate paleontologist and postdoctoral researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm. Only two gharial species exist today — found in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia — but the lineage’s fossil record spans the globe, with specimens uncovered in places including the United Kingdom, Sweden, Italy, Egypt and Japan, Burke said in an email. A glimpse of prehistoric Egypt Gharials, or gavials, are characterized by their long, slender snouts. The two living species include the critically endangered Indian gharial, Gavialis gangeticus, and the endangered false gharial, Tomistoma schlegelii. The false gharial gets its moniker from its resemblance to the Indian gharial, despite being a different species. The fossils analyzed in the new study, including the skull and five other specimens, were initially classified in 1927 as the previously named extinct species Tomistoma cairense based on their resemblance to the living false gharial. However, after performing evolutionary analyses to assess the relationships of extinct and living crocodilians, and computed tomography or CT scanning to peer inside the skull, the study authors found that the remains did not belong to the genus Tomistoma. “It was already known and recognised as something distinct, but more detailed work was needed to resolve exactly what it represented,” said co-lead study author Philip Mannion, a professor of paleobiology at the University College London. Instead, the crocodilian’s features represent a new genus, Herugavialis. Burke, who was reconstructing fossil gharials for his doctoral project, noted the subtle differences between the unidentified species and the false gharial, and started to work on an up-to-date description in December 2023. Herugavialis had razor-sharp, pointed teeth “which, alongside their long, thin snout would have been adapted to capture fish,” Burke said in an email. “The Mokattam Formation, where Herugavialis was recovered from, preserves several species of bony and cartilaginous fish fossils, which Herugavialis likely fed on.” The semiaquatic predator’s eyes would have also protruded from the skull, similar to the Indian gharial, because the eye sockets were raised like a telescope, Burke added. The Herugavialis skull may have not been discovered within the Great Sphinx itself, but the statue and the pyramids are known to be troves for both ancient Egyptian and prehistoric finds. Scientists have previously discovered hundreds of thousands of smaller fossilized organisms, such as bivalves and foraminifera — tiny creatures that lived in Egypt’s past marine ecosystem — embedded within the grand monuments. “It’s probable that larger fossils are also present within the walls of these monuments and I think it’s very likely that other fossils will continue to be found in this formation, especially of animals that like shallow marine environments,” Mannion said in an email, adding that prehistoric turtles could be a potential example. The vast fossil collection unearthed from the Mokkattam Formation reveal the rich ecosystem and the wide diversity of species that once lived in prehistoric Egypt, he said. Identifying Herugavialis from a nearly centuries-old fossil find also highlights the importance of reevaluating museum collections. “There are other fossils in similar situations, but often this is just about time and resources, both for researchers and curators, rather than that no-one is aware of their existence,” Mannion said. Reclassifying the crocodile species “helps paint a better picture of what large predators were like in the region,” said Alex Hastings, the Fitzpatrick Chair of Paleontology at the Science Museum of Minnesota in Saint Paul, who was not involved with the study. “This expands the known variety of forms of these amazing long-snouted crocodylians across the Mediterranean in ancient times and gives us better understanding for how that would have influenced ecosystems during the greenhouse environment of the Eocene,” Hastings said in an email, referring to the period from about 56 million to 34 million years ago when global temperatures were much warmer than today. Herugavialis, like many other species, had initially been assigned to a living genus even though the croc was alive a long time ago, he noted. “Studies like this provide crucial data that allows us to realize the real diversity and evolutionary background of these creatures rather than lumping them into living systems.”

cnn.com.title: Facing Russian stonewalling, Trump admin ramps up pressure for info as it struggles to plan for potential plague fallout
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and has formally escalated its request for information from the country, amid days of stonewalling from Russian officials about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the episode. The death of the technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia immediately raised alarms throughout the administration, prompting a race to compile intel and plot for a potential public health response, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. But Russia’s reluctance to share information about the incident has complicated those efforts, leaving officials uncertain what broader risks it could pose — and how exactly to defend the US against them. The US escalated its request for information, issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, a source familiar told CNN late Tuesday. “We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson said. “We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.” “It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier Tuesday. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.” US officials were in touch with the Russian government as early as last Friday, a State Department official said, including contact between the department’s health experts and the Russian Foreign Ministry. And that outreach has continued, an administration official said, as Rubio expressed hope Tuesday that the limited information sharing “will change in the next few hours and days.” President Donald Trump told reporters outside the White House Tuesday afternoon that he had “call scheduled” to speak with Russian leader Vladimir Putin about the issue “very soon.” He added US agencies would have more information to report “probably tomorrow.” But the US has gotten limited cooperation so far. What little information has come out of Russia has faced deep skepticism, with officials unconvinced that the Kremlin is being fully forthcoming, according to people familiar with the situation. Still, until the administration knows more through intelligence collection and diplomatic outreach, officials are not taking steps such as putting travel restrictions into place to prevent any potential spread, according to a US official. The US already advises against travel to Russia due to various factors, including the possibility of wrongful detention and the war with Ukraine. Among the critical questions still outstanding: whether the 28-year-old lab worker who died last week contracted pneumonic plague — a severe but treatable infection — or another, unknown infectious disease. Staff at the Anti-Plague Institute study a range of other dangerous diseases, including cholera, anthrax and brucellosis, according to the institute’s website. US officials have also sought details on whether the disease was modified in any way, a process called gain of function that could dramatically alter the way the US and other countries might respond. Rubio and other Trump officials have publicly downplayed the immediate threat to Americans, emphasizing that the administration is closely monitoring the situation and that pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics. But behind the scenes, there is deep unease within the administration over the continued lack of insight, the people familiar with the situation said. Compounding those concerns is the Russian government’s outsized response, including quarantining the hospital where the lab worker was treated, according to the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district. Nearly 200 people are under observation, a regional news outlet reported. “We don’t know a lot right now about what actually happened,” said one US official. “But one thing most of us feel certain about: The Russians are going to act like the Chinese did with Covid. They won’t be forthcoming.” Still, Trump on Monday characterized the situation as a “big problem” for Russia, suggesting that the US might need to provide some unspecified level of aid. In a statement, a State Department spokesperson said that several federal agencies were “closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague,” but that many of the details surrounding it remained unconfirmed. They reiterated that Americans have long been advised not to travel to Russia for any reason. “We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the spokesperson said. In the days since the lab worker’s death, the National Security Council and State Department officials have led the administration’s push to gather information, piece together what happened and evaluate the potential risks, officials and others familiar with the situation said. Federal health agencies, including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, have also been involved in the cross-government effort. A source familiar with the outreach said Trump officials have also backchanneled with the World Health Organization — the international health body that Trump pulled funding from soon after taking office, but that the government has continued to communicate with in emergency situations. WHO said Monday that it was in contact with Russian authorities to verify details about the lab worker’s death, though it has so far also received little information. “If they’re not transparent, if they’re not open to independent accountability, how is it possible to trust the Kremlin is telling us the full and accurate information?” said Lawrence Gostin, a global health law professor at Georgetown University who has worked closely with WHO. “Clearly, on its face, the lab was conducting extremely high-risk research and using shoddy biosafety measures.” The Anti-Plague Institute’s relatively remote location in eastern Russia, combined with the pneumonic plague’s limited ability to quickly spread, has given health experts some comfort that any immediate threat can be contained. Pneumonic plague is a bacterial infection, unlike the highly transmissible coronavirus strain that sparked the 2020 pandemic. And while the plague is fatal if untreated, there are now effective and widely available antibiotics to treat it. While there is little indication that the incident will touch off another global health crisis, officials and outside experts said it has nevertheless reinforced how difficult it can be to monitor and prepare for potential biological threats. The Health and Human Services Department may have the medical stockpile necessary to combat conventional pneumonic plague, those officials and experts said. But there’s little certainty whether it could do the same against a modified version — or how long it would take to develop a treatment if needed. Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the episode also comes as health response capabilities both in the US and globally have been diminished by funding cuts and the strain of responding to other crises. WHO has proposed slashing its budget following a $600 million shortfall triggered by the US’ exit. America’s ability to handle a new public health response, meanwhile, “is severely diminished” amid its efforts to combat measles outbreaks, she said. “We are talking about a very depleted system. God forbid you layer another pathogen onto the already laborious and difficult work of going after measles,” said Nuzzo. “That would be a nightmare.” This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego was incoherent, not malicious
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump says many bizarre and even hateful things. But signaling he would allow Iran to nuke Los Angeles and San Diego is not one of them. During a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump “weaved” his way right into a controversy that had critics, some in the media and even a GOP congressional candidate accusing him of rhetorically conceding major population centers on the West Coast to America’s sworn enemy. And you could be forgiven for reading the president’s comments that way. But context and recent history make clear that Trump’s crime was less indifference to the fate of Californians and more his increasingly profound incoherence. Which, to be clear, is still a major problem for the most powerful man in the world. First, let’s recap what Trump said. “They can take out a city,” he said of Iran. “Let them take – let it – let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s – this is a very small price to pay.” It wouldn’t be totally out of character for this to be another Trumpian verbal excess, given his recent past. This is a president who has repeatedly spoken about withholding disaster aid from states that vote against his party, and he has demonstrated some indifference to blue states. His Energy Department recently admitted in court that it canceled clean energy grants “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state.” Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont accused Trump of saying the small price to pay was the “annihilation of two major American cities.” Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called it “such a sick, evil thing to say.” Even GOP congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who serves on the San Diego County board of supervisors, said what Trump did was “write off American cities as an acceptable price of war.” Desmond “vehemently” disagreed with it. But that is pretty clearly not what Trump was trying to say. For one, immediately before the above quote, he had been talking about other costs of the Iran war — apparently referring to gas prices — being that “small price to pay.” “And again, remember — with the word — it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high,” Trump said. “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.” (You can see Trump’s full speech here.) Trump didn’t initially say he was referring to gas prices, mind you (though he did say that later). But this is precisely how he’s been talking about them for a long time — as a “small price to pay” for preventing a nuclear Iran: Also, three days ago, Trump made a very similar argument to the one he made about Los Angeles and San Diego — except about Mobile, Alabama, during a rally there. “But remember about the oil: You’re paying a price, but boy, is that a small price than what it would be if these lunatics were allowed to have a nuclear weapon and used it on Mobile, Alabama,” Trump said. “OK, not going to happen.” At his Nebraska rally, Trump basically took that talking point and made it a whole lot more unintelligible. He bounced around from talking about Kamala Harris and the election, to wanting total victory in Iran, to talking about gas prices being high (but without actually saying “gas prices”). When he made the comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego, he used very unfortunate sentence construction that did sound a lot like he would “let them” — Tehran, that is — nuke the two blue state cities. And then he returned to the gas prices — but again, in an extremely confusing way. “But it’s gonna end very soon, and it’ll end one way or the other, and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things —” Trump said, before jumping off on a tangent about Venezuela. It was so confusing that not only did that GOP congressional candidate seem to interpret it in the worst way; so did many in the crowd. Indeed, the ugliest part of this whole episode is that people actually cheered when Trump floated the destruction of Los Angeles and San Diego. That would seem to say something about the movement Trump has cultivated. But while he wasn’t advocating that, his phrasing does point to a growing problem. A president is someone you count on to be authoritative and clear, especially when talking about issues of the utmost importance like nuclear war. But Trump’s rhetoric is often anything but. Look at any recent interview where a transcript is released. Some of Trump’s responses in his Time magazine interview last week, for example, are virtually impenetrable. (Just do a word search for “unintelligible” if you want some examples.) It often feels like he’s engaging in a lengthy bout of free association. Trump has long spoken like this, to an extent. And by casting his meandering soliloquies as “the weave,” he’s tried to make it sound intentional, allowing his supporters to believe it’s his secret rhetorical genius. But the “weave” is getting harder to follow — with potentially harmful consequences, too.

cnn.com.title: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
cnn.com.text: A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty on Tuesday in Virginia to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars worth over $40 million, according to court records. David J. Rush fabricated a “highly classified” government program to justify the acquisition of luxury property in south Florida that he intended to resell for personal profit, according to a court filing. Rush separately concocted a bogus “sensitive government activity” to obtain the gold bars, the filing says. Rush’s fraudulent conduct cost the federal government approximately $194 million in total losses, according to the Justice Department. Prosecutors also accuse Rush of lying to colleagues and government contractors about his military and academic credentials and the fake program that he invented, falsely claiming it was authorized by high-ranking US officials. “Rush used his legitimate government authority and manufactured personal bona fides to create confidence in his directions,” the court filing says. Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, court records show. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff is scheduled to sentence Rush on Jan. 28 in Alexandria, Virginia. Several months ago, Rush tried to fraudulently authorize the release of $100 million from a government contract, according to Tuesday’s filing. He directed somebody else to transfer approximately $145 million to a holding company formed at his direction, then used those funds to acquire four “luxury” properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, the filing says. In previous court filings, prosecutors said Rush stashed roughly $46 million worth of gold bars from the federal government at his Virginia home. They also accused him of fraudulently claiming tens of thousands of dollars in compensation for military leave after he was honorably discharged from the US Navy in 2015. “Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency immediately referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation turned up evidence of Rush’s crimes. “David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. Rush was arrested after investigators searched his home and seized approximately 300 gold bars, roughly $2 million and about 35 luxury watches, according to an FBI agent’s affidavit. A judge ordered Rush to be held without bond after his initial court appearance earlier this year. During a hearing in June, defense attorney Jessica Carmichael said Rush wasn’t charged initially with any crimes related to the discovery of the gold bars, which she referred to as “basically a nonissue” and “nothing more than a sensational tidbit.” She said her client properly obtained the gold bars and kept them locked in a safe in his basement. “Mr. Rush never claimed they were his,” Carmichael said. Carmichael declined to comment on Rush’s guilty plea after Tuesday’s hearing. Authorities say Rush lied about his education and military background on job applications, falsely claiming to be a former Navy pilot who graduated with a bachelor’s degree from Clemson University in South Carolina and a master’s degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in New York. Investigators determined that he didn’t serve as a Navy pilot and didn’t attend either school. Rush enlisted in the Navy in 1997 and was honorably discharged from the US Navy Reserve as a lieutenant in 2015, according to the FBI affidavit.

cnn.com.title: US resident arrested in connection with Canada’s Tumbler Ridge school shooting
cnn.com.text: US authorities have arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. James Cody Bryant was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded. Bryant appeared in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle. CNN has reached out to Bryant’s lawyer for comment. A hearing has been set for October 20. Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle. The money Bryant gave the shooter amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so and refused, according to a complaint filed in court on Friday. Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. An affidavit within the complaint includes excerpts of chat logs between Bryant and Van Rootselaar on the Discord website. “I read a lot of court documents, including some that discuss incredibly heinous acts of violence, but this complaint was particularly difficult to read,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington at the Tuesday press conference, “in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned.” In one exchange, Van Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant that she wanted to “avoid doing a school” but that “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.” According to the affidavit, Bryant responded in turn that attacking a hotel “seems like a good idea.” After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school. Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference. Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.” “As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.” It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead up to the massacre. Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned. CNN’s Josh Campbell, Paula Newton and Lex Harvey contributed reporting. This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Trump admin blocks Democratic Gov. Wes Moore from speaking at Maryland shipbuilding event
cnn.com.text: Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said President Donald Trump blocked him from speaking at a Tuesday event near Baltimore meant to unveil a new multi-billion-dollar investment in submarine manufacturing. A White House official did not dispute the account. Moore played a role in negotiating the deal, which involved bringing the defense tech firm Anduril to a former steel plant on the Patapsco River to make components for Virginia-class submarines. The Navy is awarding the firm a $2.9 billion contract. Trump is planning to visit the facility and give a speech on the investment Tuesday afternoon. But Moore and other Maryland Democrats won’t be in attendance after the administration blocked the governor from speaking. “If the president of the United States wants to bring the circus in town and tell me that I’m not allowed to speak, despite the fact we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted while I go back to the work of the people of Maryland,” Moore told reporters Tuesday. A White House official said Trump had “graciously” invited Moore to the unveiling event, but only as a guest. “It’s unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump,” the official said. A spokesman for Moore said the governor “has always said he will work with anyone when it comes to delivering for Marylanders but bow to no one when it comes to standing up for them.” “The Governor is proud to welcome Anduril to Baltimore County and the thousands of permanent jobs this investment is bringing to our state,” the spokesman said. Speaking in the pre-program ahead of Trump’s remarks, co-founder and CEO of Anduril Industries Brian Schimpf thanked several people who helped make the announcement possible, including Moore, Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier. “Gov. Moore, County Executive Klausmeier, the federal congressional delegation, as well as state and local leaders throughout Maryland have all moved with urgency to help bring industrial investment at this scale to Baltimore County,” Schimpf said. “They’ve also worked closely with us across the many requirements necessary to make this investment come to fruition.” Trump and Moore have had an acrimonious history — the president tried to bar the Democrat from a governors dinner at the White House last year. Moore is considered a potential 2028 presidential candidate. This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: The biggest signs that Trump and the GOP are panicking about the midterms
cnn.com.text: Republicans have had reason to worry about the 2026 midterm elections for a while now. But there are growing signs that their fears are spilling over into panic — and that the GOP, including President Donald Trump, senses things could get really bad. That doesn’t mean things will turn out that way. And there are plenty of examples of parties overzealously slamming the panic button late in the campaign. But the Trump-era GOP has generally been a rather sanguine political party, and what we’ve seen in recent days and weeks is anything but. Trump has insisted Republicans will do well and that the many polls suggesting otherwise are wrong. But his actions increasingly point in a different direction: The GOP was already playing defense in five states Trump won by between 11 and 16 points, with the most recent addition being Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 points two years ago and that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932. But adding Nebraska and especially South Carolina to the mix is particularly striking. And in case you thought Trump’s comments about South Carolina weren’t strategic, the GOP is sending $5 million to the Palmetto State to shore up Graham. Trump allies have also told CNN they are worried about the senator’s polling. One of the most telling signs of broader GOP panic? Republicans feeling compelled to distance themselves from Trump even in these red areas — whether calling for an end to the Iran war, overhauling their websites to erase mentions of the president, or declining to campaign with Trump. On Monday, the Houston Chronicle reported that Texas Gov. Greg Abbott won’t appear with Trump when the president visits San Antonio this week. Abbott’s campaign blamed scheduling conflicts, but these are the kinds of events GOP candidates would never have missed once upon a time, especially in a red state. And indeed, many of the worst signs for the GOP are emanating from Texas. There’s the awkward ad from Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s estranged wife (who has accused him of infidelity) in which she encourages people to vote Republican. There are the leaked audio clips in which Paxton is heard complaining about Trump and the national GOP hurting his campaign. And on Monday, GOP state Rep. Briscoe Cain posted on X: “If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races go blue.” Just to underscore how stunning that would be, Democrats haven’t won any statewide race in Texas since 1994. And this isn’t some moderate Republican spouting off; this is a MAGA lawmaker who tried to help overturn the results of the 2020 election for Trump. None of this means the GOP is doomed. While there are enough signs in the polling to cause the party to worry, Democrats’ path to the Senate majority still goes through those double-digit Trump states. That’s a high bar to clear. And, we’ve seen before how parties can spend late money in lower-tier races that don’t wind up being particularly close. Back in 2020, Democrats spent some real money in Kansas, and the GOP sent money to bolster South Carolina; Republicans wound up winning those states by 11 and 10 points, respectively. Even some Democrats are pretty circumspect about their chances in South Carolina this year. But the increased desperation ahead of November 3 means it could be a long four weeks for the GOP.

cnn.com.title: Top Democrat is investigating Jared Kushner’s financial investments after CNN report
cnn.com.text: A top Democratic lawmaker is seeking information on Jared Kushner’s financial investments following a CNN investigation last week that found his private equity firm is the largest shareholder in an Israeli company backing businesses involved in Israel’s military campaigns. Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee, sent Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, a letter on Monday saying Democrats on the committee were “investigating the unprecedented and dangerous ways in which President Trump and his family have profited directly from their access to power. “…I request detailed information about your business dealings in the Middle East to understand whether your significant financial gains have come at the cost of Americans’ safety and security, ” the California representative wrote. The letter is yet another sign that House Democrats are poised to investigate President Donald Trump’s family members’ business dealings overseas and in the US, should they retake the majority in the midterm elections this fall. An attorney for Kushner dismissed Garcia’s criticisms and sought to draw attention to the congressman’s own holdings in investments scrutinized in CNN’s report on Kushner – Phoenix Financial, an Israeli financial services firm which counts Affinity Partners as its biggest investor, and Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer. “Rep. Garcia’s letter is a masterclass in irony: A member of Congress questioning a private citizen for having an interest in the same stock in which the member also holds an interest,” the attorney said in a statement to CNN. “Jared has no role in deciding what Phoenix buys or sells. But if that doesn’t matter to Rep. Garcia, he should begin by investigating himself.” Garcia’s most recent disclosure forms indicate his pension plans are managed through the California Public Employees’ Retirement System and California State Teachers Retirement System. Both plans hold stock in Phoenix Financials or Elbit Systems. A spokesperson for Garcia said Kushner’s attorney was trying to “deflect” from his client’s own conduct, adding the congressman does not trade stocks and, like the millions of other public employees in the pension plan, does not have any control over the fund and cannot opt out. Kushner “makes millions with no accountability all while he travels the Middle East on behalf of his father in law,” said Sara Guerrero, Garcia’s spokesperson. “The apparent conflict of interest between Affinity Partners’ investments and your work in the Middle East, and in particular the potential for corrupt dealmaking given those competing interests, demands congressional oversight and accountability,” Garcia’s letter stated. CNN’s investigation raised questions about potential conflicts of interest between Kushner’s volunteer role as a peace envoy to the Middle East, and his firm’s financial investments. Kushner’s attorney did not address his client’s role as a negotiator on behalf of the Trump administration. As part of the review into Kushner’s financial holdings, CNN used Israeli financial transparency laws to trace investments made by Phoenix Financial, a Tel Aviv-based firm that Kushner’s Affinity Partners doubled its stake in last year, shortly before Trump returned to the Oval Office. CNN’s reporting specifically excluded Phoenix’s investments through retirement accounts and focused on insurance holdings instead. Those records, which include only some of Phoenix’s holdings, show Phoenix has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into Elbit Systems. Phoenix also holds stakes in at least eight other companies providing equipment for the Israeli military ranging from drones and warships to demolition machinery, CNN found. All nine companies identified by CNN saw their stock value climb last year, with many stating the war in Gaza had driven demand for their businesses. Affinity doesn’t directly hold a stake in the nine companies CNN identified – but it does stand to reap rewards when Phoenix makes a profit. Kushner described Phoenix as Affinity’s “best investment” in September 2025. CNN found no indication that Kushner’s actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed. Kushner’s attorney told CNN his client has “never participated in or directed Phoenix’s decisions” on where to invest. A day after CNN’s reporting, Kushner posted a rare response on X, calling CNN’s story “deeply misleading.” Kushner did not point to any inaccuracies in the piece in his post. “Misleading stories will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace. That work is too important,” Kushner wrote on X. Garcia referenced Kushner’s social media post, writing “despite your denial of improper behavior, the fact remains that you have been allowed to hold a position of enormous power and responsibility, exempt from financial disclosure requirements and outside oversight.” In addition to CNN’s report, the New York Times published a story detailing additional “intermingling” between Kushner’s volunteer diplomatic role and his businesses, as it related to the war in Ukraine. US talks with Russia to end that war have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar deal selling oil assets from one of Russia’s biggest energy companies to a group of investors with ties to Steve Witkoff and Kushner, the two main negotiators for the Trump administration, according to the Times. A spokeswoman for Witkoff told the Times he “has no conflict of interest or financial stake in this matter” and said his work for the US administration is undertaken “at his own expense.” Kushner’s attorney did not respond to CNN’s inquiry about this reporting. Garcia and other Democrats have for years demanded answers from the White House and Trump’s family about concerns over “apparent influence peddling and quid pro quo deals” and whether foreign money is being used “to buy access to the President and influence American policy.” In March, Garcia and Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden specifically requested information from the White House about Affinity Partners’ fundraising in the Middle East – Kushner secured a $2 billion investment for his firm from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in 2021— in light of Kushner’s government work. Neither Kushner nor Affinity Partners responded to the congressmen’s earlier request. The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is the main investigative committee in the House but the minority party requests from lawmakers on the committee are voluntary and can be ignored without legal consequences. Subpoenas can only be authorized by the committee chair or by committee vote. If the balance of power shifts as a result of the midterm elections in November, Democrats would be able to open an official investigation. After Republicans won the House in 2023, the Oversight Committee, the Judiciary Committee and the Ways and Means Committee opened similar investigations into Hunter Biden’s business dealings overseas and alleged he was profiting from his father’s presidency. This story was updated with additional details from Garcia’s letter and further context on his holdings.

cnn.com.title: Someone may have hacked the North Korean UN mission’s voicemail
cnn.com.text: For the past 29 years, one of the few ways to get in touch with the North Korean government has been a phone number printed in the United Nations member directory. It’s the line to North Korea’s permanent mission to the UN — their only diplomatic outpost on American soil — an office on the 13th floor of a midtown Manhattan skyscraper. However, sometime within the past three years, an unknown person apparently hacked the mission’s voicemail, rerecording the greeting message as a satirical monologue about mass starvation and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. CNN discovered the voicemail in late September while attempting to contact the mission. Callers who dial its number and stay on for the voicemail greeting now hear a high-pitched voice speaking in a racist caricature of an East Asian accent. The speaker jokes about North Korea’s chronic food shortages and encourages anyone wishing to contact Kim Jong Un to leave a message, saying that if they do, perhaps “someone (will) get fed sometime soon.” Then an automated voice chimes in, informing the caller that the mailbox is full. Isolated North Korea has in the past faced huge food shortages driven by economic mismanagement and exacerbated by official clampdowns on border trade, as well as the diversion of scarce resources to military projects, according to experts. The North Korean mission did not answer an email inquiring about its voicemail greeting being changed. When a CNN producer went to their office in New York and knocked on the door to ask in person, a male staffer emerged. The staffer refused to answer questions but listened, with a surprised expression, as the producer called the mission’s number and played the voicemail greeting in its entirety. “This is not our number,” the staffer said and slammed the door shut. Days later, after North Korea’s vice foreign minister addressed the UN General Assembly, the mission published the phone number in question on the first page of the minister’s speech. As of writing, the greeting remains unchanged. A spokesperson for the UN Media and Liaison Unit (MALU) told CNN that the number connected to the voicemail was the only one they had, and that they were unaware of any change to the mission’s voicemail greeting. The UN’s Protocol and Liaison Service, which publishes the directory, referred CNN back to MALU. Cheap trick It’s unclear who pulled the prank, though there are a few public hints as to when it may have changed and how. David Maxwell, vice president at the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy, told CNN that he called the mission while attending a protest outside in November 2023. Maxwell recalled that the voicemail greeting at the time was just a recording informing the caller that the number did not take messages. Experts told CNN that finding out who changed the voicemail is impossible without access to the private call logs for the North Korean mission, but a stranger may have been able to re-record the mission’s greeting message without much effort. Barcelona-based cybersecurity researcher Martin Vigo told CNN that many users often fail to change their voicemail passwords from the default code issued by the carrier, which in some cases may be the last four digits of their phone number. Guessing passcodes is also rather easy, especially with automated calling services that can rapidly guess and input thousands of combinations for four-digit PINs. “For 40 bucks, I can 100% access your voicemail if you have a four-digit pin,” said Vigo. “It’s very cheap, and very fast.” ‘The New York channel’ The mission’s phone line once served as a key circuit for diplomacy. North Korea and the US have no formal ties, so the country’s UN mission long acted as “the New York channel”: one of the only points of contact between the US government and Pyongyang. Joel S. Wit, a former State Department official and author of a book on US attempts to disarm North Korea, said that the mission was an important part of negotiations over North Korea’s nuclear program in 1994. The mission has a permanent staff of 23 diplomats and aides, according to the UN’s directory. Wit remembers the mission’s office space as sparsely furnished with “the required picture of their leaders” hanging on the wall. All the mission staff live nearby, as the State Department requires North Korea’s diplomats to obtain permission before traveling more than 25 miles from New York City. “Back in the Clinton years, we were actually doing negotiations with the North Korean mission,” said Wit. “This was a very serious relationship.” But times have changed. Wit said that as succeeding attempts to defuse North Korea’s nuclear program have failed — including landmark talks in 2019 between Kim Jong Un and US President Donald Trump – Pyongyang and the US have lost what few diplomatic ties they had. Instead, North Korea has cultivated relations closer to home, especially with Russia, which has gladly accepted thousands of North Korean soldiers for the front lines of its war in Ukraine. “Ukraine is a prime example of the shift in relations,” Wit said. “The North Koreans think geopolitically. They’re not ideological robots. Their geopolitics drives their foreign policy.” “I’m sure that the New York channel today is pretty much non-functioning,” Wit continued. “Whoever hacked (the voicemail) probably didn’t know, but it’s a function of the relationship between the United States and North Korea. Today, the relationship doesn’t matter to the North Koreans.”

cnn.com.title: Checklists, masks and mystery: What we know about the plague scare in Russia
cnn.com.text: Russian authorities have sought to allay global worries over the death of a young woman who worked at a Siberian anti-plague laboratory. But moves to isolate her contacts and introduce new disease-control measures at local hospitals have raised concerns among people who fear they’re not being told the full story. The woman was a lab technician at Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in Russia’s southeast. Questions have swirled around what illness she contracted and why Russian authorities have rushed to isolate her contacts, while downplaying the suggestion that she died of plague. CNN has learned that a local maternity hospital is subjecting patients to comprehensive health checks and requiring them to fill out questionnaires about suspicious symptoms related to “plague” and other infectious diseases. Ulyana Gavryunina, a 29-year-old blogger from Angarsk, a city in the Irkutsk region, told CNN she had to change maternity hospitals at 40 weeks pregnant after newly imposed quarantine restrictions meant her husband could no longer be with her during labor. When she arrived for a scheduled appointment at the Irkutsk City Perinatal Center, her mother, who usually accompanied her during visits, was refused entry. Staff checked her temperature, asked her to show her tongue and instructed her to wear a mask, sanitize her hands and complete two questionnaires. One of them was titled “Checklist for Suspected Highly Dangerous Infectious Disease Plague” and listed symptoms such as high fever and chest pain. Staff did not mention plague, she said, telling her only that there was an unidentified “new virus” and that extra precautions were needed to protect the babies. Inside the hospital, the atmosphere was calm, Gavryunina said. “Everything was as usual,” she told CNN. “Everyone was wearing masks, that’s all.” Her biggest concern was being told her husband could no longer accompany her during labor, even if he underwent additional medical tests. For other residents, the hospital restrictions have fueled questions about whether authorities are being transparent. “It feels like they’re not telling us the whole story,” one person who self-identified as an Irkutsk resident commented beneath one of Gavryunina’s social media posts. “They’re telling everyone that it wasn’t the plague but pneumonia. Yet hospitals are still under quarantine, and ambulance doctors are driving around in full Covid protective suits.” Another local resident, who identified herself only as Ekaterina, said life there was continuing as normal. She told CNN that while some of her acquaintances were “slightly panicking,” she had seen little change on the streets. “Everything is as usual, no visible changes,” Ekaterina said. But in local Telegram groups, many expressed skepticism. “Who are you telling these fairy tales to?” one user asked. What prompted these measures? A lab worker, identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, was hospitalized on September 29, according to independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikala. She is believed to have died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town about 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk, at the end of last week. A friend of hers told CNN she died on October 2. The friend didn’t confirm any other details. Unverified reports suggest she fell ill after a potential lab-leak or contracted the illness after traveling to another region. Russia’s health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said she died of a pneumonia of “unknown” origin. The agency downplayed suspicions that her illness was related to her work. So how did the plague scare originate? The first sign of a potential issue came on October 2, when Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev posted on Telegram that Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, had convened an “extraordinary meeting” about a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection” in a resident of the region. Kobzev did not mention plague, but Alexey Tsydenov, the head of neighboring Buryatia, raised that possibility when he said in a statement that the woman “died of plague in the Irkutsk region.” According to Russian media reports, his statement was later edited to say that she had “possibly died from plague.” We don’t know what the lab worker was suffering from, or how she contracted her illness, but the opaque Russian response has fueled speculation. How have Russian authorities responded?
