Russia’s health watchdog has reassured locals that the “epidemiological situation” is stable, but local media reported that 60 workers in the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute were in quarantine and a that number of hospitals were subject to restrictions The Kremlin has urged people to rely on updates from the health watchdog rather than “various rumors and speculation.” When pressed for further information on Tuesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov again referred journalists to the health watchdog, noting it “continues its work.” But the watchdog has released limited information. What has been the international response? US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin “very soon” to discuss the deceased researcher. Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia to share more information about the circumstances of the researcher’s death. “I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.” The World Health Organization said it was in contact with Russian health authorities to “verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results.” “Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” it said. World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Tuesday that Russian health authorities reported that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk region, in response to WHO’s verification request. He said Russian health authorities told WHO that an epidemiological investigation was conducted, and contacts were identified, tested and put under medical observation. The Russian health authorities did not detect any high-threat pathogens among the contacts, Tedros said. Border measures Despite such reassurances, several countries in the region have said they are monitoring and have put safeguard measures in place. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have implemented quarantine controls at state border crossing points. Uzbekistan said it has “increased the readiness” of authorities to deal with highly infectious diseases. But there do not appear to be additional border measures in place in China, which has a history of infectious disease control with Russia. No flights from Irkutsk to China have been cancelled in recent days, according to data from Flightradar24 reviewed by CNN. Inbound and outbound travel through Heihe Port – a major border crossing connecting China’s northeast Heilongjiang province with the Russian city of Blagoveshchensk – remains normal, a salesperson at Heihe China Travel Agency told CNN on Wednesday. They had not received any notices about border controls. CNN has asked China Customs and its foreign ministry whether Beijing plans to establish any border measures. China is currently observing an national holiday. Why was the lab studying the plague? According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East. The institute was established in 1934 to combat plague and continues to study the disease because Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, still circulates naturally in wildlife across parts of Siberia and neighboring regions.

cnn.com.title: A Republican in a district Kamala Harris won could give Democrats a run for their money
cnn.com.text: Mike Lawler is one of the most vulnerable Republicans in Congress this election cycle, one of only three representing a district that Kamala Harris won in 2024. But in a year when political headwinds seem to be blowing in Democrats’ favor, combat veteran and Biden administration alum Cait Conley may still be facing an uphill battle to oust the two-term incumbent from his seat in New York’s Hudson Valley. While active registered Democrats outnumber Republicans in the 17th District by more than 70,000, according to the New York State Board of Elections, Lawler has shown crossover appeal as he has sought to highlight his bipartisan bona fides and willingness to break with President Donald Trump. That includes several endorsements from across the aisle, including Maine Rep. Jared Golden and local Democratic politicians. Senior Republicans feel confident in Lawler’s ability to maintain his seat, and House GOP leaders believe that he is one of their strongest battleground candidates and can defy the national environment. In a sign of the high stakes, the showdown has become one of the most expensive House races in the country, with Republicans and Democrats funneling more than $40 million cumulatively into ads tying Lawler to Trump and scrutinizing Conley’s connections to AI companies. But Conley still believes she can flip the seat, which could prove consequential as Democrats look to retake the House for Trump’s final two years in power. “The energy that we are feeling in every corner of this district is incredible,” she told CNN during a campaign event on Sunday. “Where people are recognizing the stakes of this November and how this is a fight for working families who are getting screwed by the policies of this administration, enabled by Mike Lawler.” ‘A long and deep history of really aggressive retail politics’ Conley, however, is still introducing herself to voters as a first-time candidate, while Lawler benefits from nearly four years of incumbency and the ensuing name recognition. In recent months, she’s tried to excite voters by campaigning with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly and highlighting endorsements from former Rep. Gabby Giffords and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will also join her on the campaign trail in the coming weeks, according to Jeffries spokesperson Justin Chermol. National Democrats are also invested in the race, with an operative for House Democrats calling the seat a top priority for the party. House Majority PAC, the super PAC linked to Jeffries, has already spent over $1.8 million in cable advertising in the race so far with further reservations in the New York City media market, HMP communications director CJ Warnke said. But what it could come down to, Democratic strategist Doug Forand says, is face time with voters. “Her challenge is to continue to work the retail side of it, you know, and that district has a long and deep history of really aggressive retail politics,” he said. Linda, a Bedford resident who voted for Harris in 2024, is still on the fence about voting in this year’s midterm election. “Other than the governors, I don’t know enough about the other people running yet,” she told CNN. But she said that her grandson, who is a Republican, is supporting Conley. “He just likes what he knows about her,” she added. Mt. Kisco resident and small business owner Steve Nadler, who also supported Harris in the last presidential election, feels similarly. “I’ll definitely do my own research prior to submitting a vote,” he said. Lawler, for his part, says he hasn’t been bothered by national attention on the race and is confident he can keep the seat. “I think the work I’ve done has put the spotlight on this race,” he said during a stop in Pleasantville, New York. “Ultimately, I don’t feel any uphill battle or additional pressure from it, I live for this.” A Republican with Democratic endorsements Despite Trump’s deep unpopularity, Lawler’s local relationships and pitch as a moderate Republican willing to work across the aisle still appear to hold sway with voters. While cost of living was a top concern for voters who spoke with CNN, few Republicans seemed to fault the Trump ally for it, despite Conley’s efforts to tie them together. “It’s a little hard when you’re a widow, you’re on Social Security, you’re retired. You know, I spend all my money paying bills,” said 77-year-old Susan Sciascia of Pleasantville. While she feels the strain on her finances, she plans to vote for Lawler next month and says he understands what Americans are experiencing. “He’s a family man. He’s got kids. He’s got a wife. He’s in it too.” Sciascia added. “He knows what he’s going through, so he knows what we’re going through.” Conley has also made affordability a central focus in her campaign, but national Democrats want her to push on this issue harder in her messaging in the final weeks of the campaign, a high-ranking aide told CNN. While Lawler has sought to highlight areas where he’s willing to break with Trump, such as in negotiations on state and local taxes, he’s also worked to tie Conley, who is running as a moderate, to the further left contingencies within her own party. During a debate last week, Lawler accused New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist and staunch critic of Israel’s government, of antisemitism, and demanded Conley denounce him. Conley said she condemned antisemitism from anyone and noted that she has disagreements with some democratic socialists within her party, before turning the subject to Trump’s impacts on the district. But just a train ride away from New York City, the 17th District has a large Jewish population and the Democratic Party’s ongoing debate over Israel could play a role in the House race. Lawler has highlighted the endorsements of two local Democratic Jewish officials, New Castle Town Councilwoman Ally Chemtob and Montebello Deputy Mayor Stacy Caridi, who cited the congressman’s efforts to fight antisemitism. “My support for Mike is personal, because when I look beyond party labels to someone I know and trust, I see someone who cares about the safety and well-being of my children,” Chemtob said in a campaign press release. Conley, however, has stressed her support for Israel and said that she would have voted against cutting military aid to the country. Asked if she wants Mamdani, or another New York City progressive, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to join her on the campaign trail this fall, Conley told CNN, “Right now, I’m just focused on voters getting to know me and meeting them everywhere that they are.” That focus was on display on an overcast Sunday last weekend, as she spoke to volunteers armed with lawn signs at a canvassing event in Armonk, New York, and acknowledged the tightness of the race. “I promise you this is going to be a fight where every door knocked, every call made, every vote is going to matter, and it is a fight that I know I can win, but I cannot win alone,” Conley said.

cnn.com.title: Whistleblower says Trump demanded FBI probe into protesters over a TikTok he saw
cnn.com.text: The FBI opened preliminary investigations targeting anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement protesters in Southern California, a former FBI intelligence official alleged in a whistleblower complaint, adding that she believed the move violated the law and agency policy. The investigations were opened in early 2025 in the early weeks of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown following demands from President Donald Trump and other administration officials, according to the disclosure by Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office. CNN reviewed the complaint, which was filed by lawyers representing Fields to members of the Senate Judiciary Committee. A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN said the DOJ will continue to “vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law.” “The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job.” A statement from the White House also suggested the investigation was focused on violent acts, which it said are not protected by the First Amendment. “These allegations are FALSE. The First Amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” CNN has also reached out to the FBI for comment. In at least one instance, the FBI began preliminary investigations of protesters after the president demanded an investigation of people he saw in a TikTok video depicting demonstrators against ICE and Customs and Border Protection in Alhambra, California. The protesters were using bullhorns to warn neighbors about the presence of immigration-enforcement officers, Fields’ disclosure said. Following the February 2025 protest in Alhambra, an analyst who worked under Fields “informed her that the squad had been ordered to run pre‑assessment checks on the two to four anti‑ICE and CBP protesters in the video accused of impeding an immigration arrest, even though FBI policy prohibits opening investigations based solely on First Amendment‑protected activity, and the squad did not yet have evidence of a crime,” lawyers representing Fields said in a letter to senators. The investigations came after FBI Director Kash Patel told top FBI leaders that the president “was angry about the incident, and he wanted those protesters investigated and arrested,” the letter said. In a letter to Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, citing the whistleblower complaint, Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla questioned the Justice Department on how many investigations into protestors were currently active and whether Trump had directed other, similar investigations. Fields’ whistleblower complaint disclosed two separate incidents in which she said White House officials demanded the FBI investigate and arrest anti-ICE protesters. A separate incident weeks earlier sparked a similar focus on free speech, according to Fields, when then-Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove demanded the FBI investigate a group of anti-ICE protestors outside a federal building in California. In both cases, Fields noted that First Amendment protections prohibited such investigations and potential charges unless other action beyond speech had taken place. When she raised the issue with one superior, Fields says she was told it had to happen. The former analyst said she was stripped of her team and lost support from FBI leadership in her Los Angeles office, pushing her to ultimately resign from the bureau. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: At Starbucks, the future could be smaller
cnn.com.text: Starbucks is on a mission to recapture its roots as a place to sit down for a cup of coffee. But it doesn’t think it needs a big footprint to deliver on that promise. A new café prototype that opened last month in San Antonio has all the features of a typical Starbucks, like plush seating, bakery treats displayed in a glass case as well as an espresso bar for baristas to make drinks. However, it’s a fraction of the size of a usual location. The new design helps Starbucks push into areas where real estate is expensive, particularly in major cities. Starbucks reworked the counter with a new “folded bar” configuration to fit into narrower spaces rather than running the entirety of a café. But the chain said the new format still has seating for people to socialize and connect, which has become a hallmark of its reinvigoration plan to recapture the “third place” energy that’s a priority for CEO Brian Niccol. “These particular new formats are really stretching us to be more adaptable to different types of location, different shapes and different sizes, but they still hold all of the aspects of the (coffee house) experience,” said Dawn Clark, the company’s senior vice president of global concepts and design. Prior to Niccol’s arrival in 2024, Starbucks largely tailored its locations to customers picking up orders off its mobile app. It pulled out 30,000 comfortable seats, installed hard wooden stools and blocked electrical outlets, making cafes a less desirable place to hang out. Sales suffered as a result, as well as for a variety of other reasons, including higher prices, longer waits for pickup orders and lackluster food options. In 2025, as part of a $1 billion restructuring effort, the chain announced a massive renovation plan that brought back cozy seating, more plugs and free refills to encourage customers to stick around. So far, around 1,000 existing locations have been redesigned in North America, with Starbucks planning to accelerate the face lifts. A smaller-sized prototype could fit into its growth plans. Smaller size Starbucks is applying aspects of its broader redesign project to this smaller prototype. It doesn’t want repeat the mistakes of the ill-fated pick-up only stores that were created for small spaces. Niccol shuttered them in July 2025, saying the locations were “overly transactional.” The sterile design didn’t have seats and encouraged people to order strictly via its mobile app. Clark used that as a case study for this design so as to not limit how people order their drinks. About 30% of customers use mobile ordering, the company says. “Customers have variable needs and they would like to be able to choose different ways of interacting with us, depending on what their day is like,” she told CNN, adding that the new locations let people order in person, for delivery, on the app and even at a drive-thru. So far, six locations of the smaller prototype are open, including in San Antonio and Manhattan. The company declined to reveal the square footage of the new design. Starbucks’ success Starbucks has had a mixed success in attracting people back to the chain. The company has closed hundreds of locations over the past two years across North America. However, same-store US sales turned positive in the most recent quarter, and it has plans to open about 5,000 new locations in the coming years. Clark said they’ve learned from the 1,000 locations they’ve remolded so far, and plan to use the information from both customers and employees in this new, smaller design. “It’s very symbiotic and we’re getting a lot of feedback that the kind of reenergizing of the coffee house is really positive for both sides.”

cnn.com.title: Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
cnn.com.text: Officials in California denounced comments made by President Donald Trump as “dangerous” on Monday after he appeared to suggest Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego — major cities in a state he has often criticized. Speaking at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, ahead of the midterm elections, Trump once again called the consequences of the war with Iran a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” adding that Iran could potentially take out an American city. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said in comments that drew swift backlash from California’s leaders. “This is a very small price to pay and it’s gonna be over with very soon,” he said of the war. Trump has repeatedly made the argument that high gas prices are a small price to pay for the war in Iran, and in his Nebraska comments, he appeared to contrast that with a dramatically higher price to pay — an attack on a US city. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said on X that Trump was “clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.” “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money,” Cheung said. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom called the president “deranged and dangerous,” while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the statements about the city “could potentially compromise our safety.” “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” said Bass, also a Democrat. The Democratic mayor of San Diego, Todd Gloria, said the city “is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” Trump’s comments also drew criticism from Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” said Desmond, who is running in California’s 48th Congressional District. He added, “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” Trump’s highlighting of cities in California that could be targeted by Iran comes as he has frequently criticized the state and its leaders over immigration, state elections and wildfires. The president also repeated during his speech in Nebraska that the war is “going to end very soon.” At the onset of the war, Trump had vowed that the conflict would only last a few weeks, but it has since gone on seven months. The president made the new argument last week that his initial four-to-six-week timeline had just been about the time it would take to eradicate the nuclear threat from Iran and not the time it would take to conclude the entire war. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Buttigieg, Gallego and other potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meeting
cnn.com.text: A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the party’s future, in one of the party’s first major gatherings following the election. Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, according to an initial lineup shared first with CNN. The group of speakers also includes Govs. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, plus several additional members of Congress. The “What’s Next” summit is being hosted from November 12-14 by Majority Democrats, an organization that launched last year to help Democrats win in more places. In staging the event less than two weeks after the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the Senate and the House, the group is looking to move quickly to outline the lessons learned from the election that could be instructive going forward, including in the next White House race. “This isn’t a policy conference nor a talk shop on tactics,” said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss, chair of Majority Democrats, in a statement. “What’s Next is timed for a unique moment after the midterms and before the presidential to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage.” Organizers chose Denver partly because it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. The initial lineup also includes top party strategists such as David Axelrod, former senior adviser to President Barack Obama and a chief political analyst at CNN; Quentin Fulks, former principal deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024; and Morris Katz, adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Majority Democrats is not the only organization holding an event in the immediate aftermath of the midterms in a bid to shape the party’s future. Two days after the election, some of the party’s most prominent strategists and commentators are set to converge in Washington, DC, for Crooked Con, which is hosted by the progressive media company Crooked Media.

cnn.com.title: Disney increases park prices every year. Here’s how it avoids pricing out families
cnn.com.text: Disney raised prices on many of its theme park offerings today, coinciding with the start of the company’s new fiscal year. But consumers aren’t pushing back the way they did a few years ago. Disney’s price hikes are an annual October ritual for the company, and it’s always a tricky balancing act between increasing revenue and consumers’ willingness to pay. Many ticket types, passes and add-ons at Disneyland are not increasing at all this time. But premium products are getting more expensive, like the highest-level, skip-the-line service at Walt Disney World, which could now run just shy of the $500 mark during peak demand. It’s a reflection of the company’s strategy: Spread the price boosts across different audiences, while leaving bottom-tier prices - like the slowest season, one-day, one-park tickets - unchanged. Its theme parks strategy, Disney said, has evolved over time. Higher-priced premium products and add-ons, alongside targeted discounts and a refresh of older attractions, allowed the company this summer to generate the strongest parks and cruises revenue in two years. The company kept entry-level prices stable this year, when many consumers are reigning in discretionary spending. “Our goal is to put guests at the center of our decision making, and that starts by listening to them,” Thomas Mazloum, chairman of Disney Experiences, told CNN ahead of the price hikes. “That matters more now when families are watching every dollar, and we see it in the choices they make every day — in how they plan, in how far ahead.” Disneyland holds relatively steady Some prices at Disneyland are inching up, like adding the option to hop between two parks in the same day ($5 to $15 more), most middle-tier Disneyland tickets (about $5 or 3% more), and its Lightning Lane Multi Pass skip-the-line service ($1 or 3% more). However, a broad slate of products at Disneyland are not increasing in price: the cheapest tickets for the slowest days of the year, the peak tickets for the busiest days of the year, multi-day tickets, parking and annual passes. The base ticket price has held steady at $104 since 2019. But for the first time in a decade, the most expensive one-day, one-park ticket for Disneyland (usually during end-of-year holidays) is also not budging from its current $224. The fact that none of the annual passes are changing in price is also a first. The relative lack of price movement this year in Anaheim, California, speaks to the main clientele: locals. Disney told CNN that visitation to Disneyland tends to be more regional with shorter stays; Disney World guests typically plan further ahead, travel longer distances, and take longer vacations. Pnina Feldman, associate professor of technology and operations management at the University of Virginia, said Californians “are deciding how many times to visit this year.” “That decision is price sensitive,” she said. Different coasts, different needs The very same items at Disney World in Florida are seeing different price treatments. “We have all kinds of guests coming through our gates,” Disney’s Mazloum said, “and it’s exactly why we think about pricing market by market, rather than with one broad brush.” Current Disney World ticket prices have been set through October 2027. But for the remainder of 2027, the new price of the peak, one-day, one-park ticket will increase by $10 to $229 plus tax. The lowest-priced, one-day, one-park ticket will stay the same at $119 plus tax. Feldman said that at Disney World, more guests are from out of state. “For guests who flew in and booked a hotel, a few dollars on a ticket rarely changes the decision to go, so the increase in price won’t fundamentally decrease demand,” she said. Annual passes to Disney World are going up by $10 to $120, depending on the pass. Middle-tier Disney World tickets, multi-day tickets, and a skip-the-line service for individual premium rides, will also see a moderate increase. The high-end version of that service that allows guests into every available fast lane without reservations could go up $50 based on demand. The price of the cheaper skip-the-line option that requires reservations, as well as parking rates, will not change. Listening to feedback Gavin Doyle, founder of third-party Disney news site MickeyVisit.com, said his readers follow the company — and the annual price increases — closely. “I’m just seeing Disney start to really listen to fan feedback in a way that they haven’t in the past, always,” Doyle said. In post-pandemic years, he said some guests felt like the changes to policies and price increases made it more difficult to visit a place over which they feel so much ownership. In response, Disney rolled back some pandemic-era decisions, such as making Disney World hotel parking free again for guests. Beci Mahnken, CEO of MEI-Travel agency, said that even in financially uncertain times, her clients aren’t foregoing Disney trips altogether. However, “some clients are willing to adjust their dates, resort or length of stay when the right offer comes along because it can make a meaningful difference in the overall cost,” Mahnken said. That’s exactly what Disney is hoping for: to use pricing to spread crowds out more evenly throughout the year, hopefully providing a better experience for all visitors. “We’re so proud that guests keep choosing us, year after year. It tells us we’re getting that balance right,” Mazloum said.

cnn.com.title: US and China discussing reciprocal nuclear site visits amid concerns about a new arms race
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration has discussed beginning reciprocal nuclear site visits with China and plans to continue pushing for that possibility during in-person meetings in the coming months, according to sources familiar with the matter. The discussions, which have been informal and preliminary, come amid mounting US concerns about China’s rapidly growing nuclear weapons program and after the last remaining arms control agreement between the US and Russia expired last year. The effort to establish a trilateral agreement began in Trump’s first term, but no tangible progress has been made and formal talks on a new accord have not begun, with China and Russia largely ignoring substantive US outreach efforts. The idea of reciprocal visits was initially raised by the Chinese while meeting US officials this year, one source said, giving some indication that the communist nation may be open to pursuing confidence building measures that could pave the way for a grander agreement. Visits to the US Department of Energy national labs and to China’s equivalent facilities were discussed, and the US would be open to discussing visits to nuclear testing sites, the source said. The nuclear discussions between the US and Chinese officials at the working level so far this year have largely occurred on the sidelines of gatherings by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, known as the P5, sources said. The concept of allowing nuclear site visits could move the needle on the US efforts to engage China on issues related to strategic stability and potentially serve as a building block for a trilateral agreement, but China remains adamant that they will not engage on discussions that could limit their nuclear buildup. The US currently has a much bigger nuclear arsenal with about 5,000 total nuclear warheads while China has about 600, but it is expanding its nuclear weapons infrastructure and has been projected to produce hundreds more warheads over the next decade. A State Department spokesperson referred questions to the White House, which did not provide a comment. CNN has requested comment from the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. Last Thursday, China began its weeklong National Day holiday, during which all government offices are closed. Paul Dean, who previously served as an acting assistant secretary of state overseeing US arms control efforts, told CNN that the administration needs to approach any Chinese nuclear negotiations with its “eyes wide open,” but said that reciprocal visits would be “an extremely valuable confidence-building measure” that could lay the informational and diplomatic foundation for additional work to reduce nuclear risk between the two countries. “This is a very dangerous time, and there are very few guardrails in place on the US-China nuclear relationship,” Dean, now a vice president at the Nuclear Threat Initiative nonprofit, said. President Donald Trump expressed support for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, Russia and China when he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, but they didn’t discuss the possibility of site visits during their talks, a US official said. Xi did not leave the door open to discussing a trilateral agreement, pointing to the US and Russian nuclear arsenals being larger than China’s – a point that Chinese officials have routinely used to shield themselves from any discussions that could lead to limiting their nuclear stockpile before they are on par with the US, the official added. Still, the topic of nuclear arms control has long been a focus for Trump, who is expected to meet with Xi twice later this year. By the time the two leaders meet again it is expected that further lower-level discussions on possible nuclear site visits will have taken place, the sources said. Visiting nuclear sites for on-site inspections have historically been used as a vital verification tool by the International Atomic Energy Agency to be sure that nations are abiding by their commitments to using the facilities for peaceful purposes. Skepticism about China’s motives Experts and former US officials who spoke with CNN were encouraged by the talks but were not confident that they will immediately lead to concrete progress on a breakthrough agreement. “It has to be taken seriously. It could be a great start,” said a former US official who has engaged China in track two discussions related to strategic stability in recent years. Still, skeptics noted that the Chinese may have floated the idea in an effort to create a positive atmosphere or to appear serious on the topic of nuclear arsenals, said former US officials and experts who questioned the authenticity of such an offer. “In advance of a big summit if the Chinese can put good feelers out there they will do that,” said another former US official who focused on nuclear issues. “It makes them seem more magnanimous as the two sides are engaging.” The Chinese may have a “maligned motivation” they said. About a year ago Trump said that the US would resume nuclear testing on an “equal basis” with China and Russia, but there has been no known US nuclear testing since that pronouncement. The administration earlier this year accused China of carrying out a secret nuclear test in 2020 using a technique known as “decoupling” designed to evade detection by firing the explosion in an empty cavern to minimize seismic shaking. The National Nuclear Security Administration’s nonproliferation directorate conducted a 16-ton underground non-nuclear explosion last week at the Nevada National Security Site that was the second in a years-long series of experiments designed to mimic the alleged Chinese test, according to an agency spokesperson. The decoupled test explosion offered NNSA and other entities a chance to validate the effectiveness of new methods and equipment for detecting such stealthy tests. “You cannot evade American innovation,” NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams said in a news release announcing the test. The Trump administration is also working on a proposal that would enable assure verification that low-yield nuclear testing is not happening at nuclear sites and could share that with the P5 group later this year, a US official said. It is unclear what kind of technical equipment could be part of that proposal. Gerald Brown, who studies China’s military at the Council on Foreign Relations nonprofit, said he is “not particularly optimistic” but that the reciprocal visit scheme, if enacted, is “a potential glimmer of hope” for reducing nuclear risk between the US and China. Brown, a former State Department intel analyst, said that China’s ongoing nuclear buildup “is deeply linked with political goals, namely its aggressive ambitions regarding Taiwan.” China historically has viewed nuclear talks as “tool to gain political concessions” on Taiwan, he argued, rather than as a genuine policy goal. “You won’t know what’s on the table until you engage in a thoughtful, rigorous way to see if this is something in our interest — and it might be,” said Dean. Dean, whose nonprofit has engaged with Chinese entities in nonofficial diplomatic discussions in recent months, said he sees mutual “interest and acknowledgement that the risks are real.” He pointed at the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which sparked some of the first US-Soviet risk reduction measures like a 24-hour phone hotline, as a historical warning. “We don’t need to wait for a crisis to start reducing nuclear risks,” Dean argued. “And the risks are very real right now.” Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

cnn.com.title: Former German spy chief arrested on treason and espionage allegations
cnn.com.text: A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor’s office said. August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement. Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage. The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for. The premises of both men were searched Tuesday. Former aide allegedly supplied Hanning with BND documents The prosecutor’s office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning’s chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026. “In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor’s office said. Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said. “The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said. Hanning used the information in private consulting work, and on one occasion “used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service.” Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information for several years, the statement said, but it was not immediately clear if the collaboration continued until their arrests on Tuesday. The office did not say which country the foreign agent worked for and said “it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient.” The statement added that “Hanning was in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years.” Hanning is suspected of involvement in a prominent child abduction case Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years. The investigation into that case led to Tuesday’s arrests. The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated. Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor’s office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa. The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court. A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned. German opposition lawmaker calls for a quick probe German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation. “This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services. “We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning,” von Notz told Spiegel Online. “We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in the Germany for years,” he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.

cnn.com.title: Nobel Prize in physics awarded to Francis Halzen for his work detecting ‘ghostly’ cosmic particles
cnn.com.text: The 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen, a pioneering Belgian astrophysicist whose work developing a massive observatory in Antarctica to detect “ghostly” cosmic particles  laid the foundations for an “entirely new type of astronomy.” These tiny, high-energy particles from space, known as neutrinos, transmit information which allow scientists to better understand distant galaxies and exploding stars, said Nobel committee member Eva Olsson at the award presentation on Tuesday at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. “Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument,” said Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce in a statement. “His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.” Halzen, 82, told the Nobel news conference by phone from Italy that it was a “great surprise” and “pleasure” to win the award. “When we started this project, everybody realized this was maybe a good idea but very few thought it would work, including myself,” he said. “So this was kind of an adventure where success wasn’t guaranteed.” The professor, who is based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, first presented plans for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in 1988, envisioning a vast network of sensors in Antarctic ice that could capture neutrinos. The observatory harnesses a key property of neutrinos — that they produce a flash of light when colliding with an atomic nucleus which could be tracked by sensors embedded in clear, glacial ice. Arriving at Earth from the far reaches of the cosmos, neutrinos are often called “ghostly” because they are extremely volatile, or vaporous, and can go through any kind of matter without changing. They have almost no mass, and no electrical charge. They can travel through the most extreme environments, like stars, planets and entire galaxies, and remain the same. “It’s been a while since the Nobel Prize has gone to a single individual and that points to the uniqueness of his vision,” said Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, which is published by the American Institute of Physics. “It took a team of hundreds of people to build it, but it all started with one person.” Observatory in the ice While billions of neutrinos originate from the sun, neutrinos that come from other regions of space are much rarer and harder to detect. In the 1980s, Halzen first realized that Antarctic ice could be ideal for trapping these secretive neutrinos but installing sensitive equipment deep in the ice was a huge endeavor requiring researchers to drill kilometer-deep holes and lower strings of light sensors. IceCube’s predecessor, known as AMANDA, was completed in 2000 but it didn’t manage to detect the high-energy neutrinos Halzen was looking for, the Nobel Committee said. Work then began on IceCube – a cubic kilometre of ice equipped with light sensors, which reached its full size in 2011, with 5,160 light sensors divided between 86 cables. In 2013, the research team reported the first evidence to support the detection of cosmic neutrinos and a couple of years later, they had gathered enough data to be certain of their discovery. The Nobel committee said IceCube would take neutrino astronomy to a new level, providing information about cosmic phenomena that are hidden behind dust clouds and distant space objects such as black holes. A project to expand IceCube, allowing it to monitor eight cubic kilometers of ice, is planned. Last year, the physics prize went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for their discovery of a phenomenon called quantum mechanical tunneling in an electrical circuit, an advance that laid the foundation for quantum computing and other related technology. The prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million). On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded to three scientists for their work developing a technique to decode the inner workings of the brain. The awards continue on Wednesday with the announcement of the chemistry prize, followed by literature on Thursday. The peace prize will be revealed on Friday, followed by the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on October 12. This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.

cnn.com.title: Wall Street is booming. Surging yields could shake things up
cnn.com.text: Wall Street rolled into 2026 on a hot streak and continued with a booming first half. Profits surged, fueled by massive spending on artificial intelligence, elevated trading activity in a volatile market and dealmaking that has benefited from a relaxed regulatory environment under the Trump administration. Wall Street hauled in $45.9 billion in profits in the first half of the year, up 51% from the same period a year ago, according to the New York State Comptroller’s latest report on the securities industry in New York City. At the current pace of growth, the industry’s profits in 2026 could exceed $90 billion for the full year — smashing through previous records and outpacing the inflation-adjusted record set in 2009. The boon for traders and bankers comes as AI investment is fueling US economic growth even as consumer sentiment hovers at historic lows due to concerns about the cost of living, from rising energy prices to stubborn food inflation. “Despite geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty, the industry has remained resilient,” Thomas P. DiNapoli, New York State Comptroller and author of the report, said in a statement. The good times are expected to keep rolling, but risks remain. The financial industry has a lingering obstacle to deal with: rising interest rates. The key 10-year Treasury yield, which sets interest rates across the economy, hit 5.35% on Monday — its highest level since 2002. The recent rise in interest rates “may dampen profitability” if dealmaking slows down or firms’ interest liabilities rise significantly, DiNapoli noted. The surge in bond yields is pushing up the cost of borrowing from mortgages to auto loans, which can weigh on economic activity. Higher yields can also raise risks for the stock market and put a chill on the hot IPO and dealmaking market. “Rising yields for bonds issued by the U.S. and other governments in recent weeks are another concerning indicator for investors,” DiNapoli wrote in the report. Wall Street rides the AI wave The New York City comptroller’s office had forecasted in May that Wall Street would earn $45.3 billion in profits for the entire year — a figure that has already been surpassed. The surge in profits has been driven by robust trading in stocks, bonds and currencies, fees from supervising and advising clients’ investments, underwriting initial public offerings and a pickup in mergers and acquisitions. “Investment in AI companies continues to drive the market,” DiNapoli wrote. AI-related venture capital spending hit $407 billion in the first half of the year, more than 50% higher than the annual total of $264 billion in 2025, the report found. The AI boom, a pickup in M&A and a series of IPOs have created a sweet backdrop for earnings. Revenues from underwriting activities — like IPOs — rose 68% year-over-year in the first half of 2026, the report found. Anthropic, a powerhouse AI company that could be valued at $2 trillion, is expected to go public this year, creating another major opportunity for Wall Street banks to haul in fees from underwriting and trading activity. Wall Street’s fortunes have also been aided by a business-friendly administration in the White House, DiNapoli said. The boosts to companies’ bottom lines are reflected in growing salaries: The average annual salary (including bonuses) in New York City’s securities industry rose 11.1% to $561,770 in 2025. The bonus pool last year reached $49.2 billion, the report found, equivalent to an average bonus of $246,900 per employee, up 6% from the previous year. Wall Street’s windfall is also a boon for New York State and City tax revenues. The industry’s contribution to New York City tax collections rose 15.8% in the 2026 fiscal year compared to the prior year. “Commensurate with record industry profitability, tax collections related to securities continue to reach new levels,” DiNapoli wrote in the report. Still, bond market volatility has picked up in recent weeks. The rise in interest rates could put pressure on Wall Street firms’ trading returns, while also dampening the outlook for the IPO market and dealmaking, as well as the consumer. Wall Street is at the center of the AI boom, but is also exposed to any downturn or fading enthusiasm. “While the industry continues to see strong profits, there are growing concerns regarding ongoing geopolitical conflicts, inflation and interest rates, the outsized contributions of the burgeoning AI sector and the deregulatory push of the current administration,” DiNapoli wrote. He added that “the potential for an industry downturn presents an increasing risk to public finances and the broader regional economy.”

cnn.com.title: The Senate is up for grabs. Plot each party’s best path to winning
cnn.com.text: As many as 10 key Senate races identified by CNN that are on the ballot in November will likely determine which party controls the chamber. Democrats need 51 seats to win majority control of the Senate. Republicans need 50 seats because Vice President JD Vance has the power to cast a tie-breaking vote for the GOP. Each party has multiple paths to Senate control. Use this interactive map to see how different hypothetical results would tip the balance. The key races, highlighted in yellow, are those most likely to be in play on Election Day. Other races in states with more predictable partisan outcomes are shaded by their current senator’s party.

bbc.com.title: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
bbc.com.text:
- Published
US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after surviving a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while "handcuffed and shackled to the bed" in hospital, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two failed lethal injections last Wednesday in Tennessee.
She was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical. Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented.
Pike is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection.
Her lawyers said her prognosis remained unclear, but that "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking.
There had been seven other cases where prisoners survived executions but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
"They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," Denno said. "This has never happened before."
Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, a local journalist who witnessed the attempted execution said that he, too, did not know of "an exact precedent".
Steven Hale, a journalist for the Nashville Banner, said the case raised many questions, including "what must this be like for the victim's family, who for 30 years has been told we are gonna give you justice and justice is us executing Christa Pike".
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong after twice injecting her with the chemical pentobarbital.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he planned to resign.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.
Pike's lawyers are scheduled to appear in court in Nashville on Wednesday. They also plan to hold a news conference outside the court.
In their latest update, they repeated their call for Lee to use his powers to commute Pike's sentence to the lower punishment of life in prison without parole.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said on Tuesday that the likelihood of recovering from lethal injection was low.
"Most people who get lethal injection die from it," he told the BBC. "In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa. So, the fact that she survived it... was unusual."
But there remains a lot of uncertainty and many unknowns, he said, including how much of the pentobarbital got into her system, what her blood levels were after the injection and what her recovery will look like.
"I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he noted.
Zivot had previously said the two doses of pentobarbital she received last week would have been enough that, had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation, "she would have surely died".
Instead, Zivot said a possible explanation is that instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
They said on Tuesday that she has endured "severe damage" to her arms.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks information about such cases.
For lethal injections, such incidents have typically occurred due to difficulty obtaining reliable IV access to the veins, though the underlying reason differs from person to person.
In cases the centre has documented, all failures happened before the lethal drugs could be administered. The last failed lethal injection that was tracked happened earlier this year - also in Tennessee.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.

bbc.com.title: Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023.
"We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi.
By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.
The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies."
As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places.
Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer.
The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire.
Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours.
"On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me.
"From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed."
An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz.
Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby.
Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later.
As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe.
The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place. "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here."
The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen.
The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here.
On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping.
Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards.
Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis.
"This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry."
"Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone."
While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed.
Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated.
Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here.
They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. Dalit and Achi are determined to return too.
"We'll come back for the memory of Shiri and for the people that didn't have the chance to live here, and for the memory of my parents, and to continue our roots, and for my children, because this is our home," Dalit says.
However, she, Achi and their children - currently displaced and living in an apartment in a town further north - face a two-year wait for Nir Oz to reopen fully.
"Terrorists penetrated 97% of the households and burned down almost 50%," says Emi Palmor, director of the rebuilding project. "Now it's the only place in Israel that has to be completely demolished and completely replanned."
She says that it is a difficult balance to redesign the kibbutz so that it feels like home but does not cause new trauma to those who return.
"It's a huge debate – a very painful debate," Emi says. "Some people say, 'If I come back here, I want the entire area to look serene. I don't have to be reminded because I remember every day the people I lost.' Other people say, 'There is such denial – if we will take down the last houses, who will ever believe?'"
About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage after an estimated 6,000 Palestinians streamed across the Gaza border during the attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN.
Despite the US-brokered ceasefire deal which brought the last hostages home a year ago, violence has continued, including near-daily Israeli attacks on Gaza. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced and much of the territory is in ruins. US President Donald Trump's peace plan is at an impasse.
For Israelis, there are outstanding questions over accountability for the failure of Israel's security forces to have prevented the 7 October attacks. People from Nir Oz favour a comprehensive state commission of inquiry and still have major security concerns.
Survivors, including the Aharons, suffer from post-traumatic stress. Dalit recalls how her eldest son, Uri, turned nine on 7 October 2023 - when they spent the day hiding in their bomb shelter. "He told me, 'Mum, I don't want to die on my birthday,'" she says. "You know people don't understand that we still live this horrible day."
This anniversary of the attacks is the first with no hostages remaining in Gaza. "It's a very big relief," Dalit says. Achi sees that now is the time to focus on personal healing.
"Until the hostages came back, it was the only thing on our mind," he says. "Now you have the time to concentrate on yourself, on what you lost, what you need. Now it's our recovery or some kind of recovery as much as we can."

bbc.com.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
bbc.com.text:
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.
"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.
While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.
Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".
The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high.
According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.
"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."
That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?
Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.
The economy looming large
There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.
But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.
Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.
When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.
"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."
He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".
In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.
When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.
But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.
Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.
It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.
"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."
Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".
"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."
And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".
"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.
Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.
For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.
The Donalds-Donald relationship
Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website.
It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself.
"Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!"
Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor.
"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor."
While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism.
Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries.
According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution.
"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic."
Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president.
The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short.
It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole.
"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job."
He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy.
The Republican messaging
In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.
"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.
According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most.
"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.
With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign.
That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.
"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"
Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.
He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike.
He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.
"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."
Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.
If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.
"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."
But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency.
